newsitem.title: SWEDEN: NATO chief says no firm decisions in 1996.
newsitem.headline: NATO chief says no firm decisions in 1996.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Wednesday no firm decision would be taken this year on the western security alliance's enlargement or future relations with Russia.
Speaking at a press conference, Solana denied Interfax news agency reports out of Moscow on Tuesday that quoted him as saying that NATO hoped to sign a treaty with Russia by the end of 1996.
"No formal signature will take place in 1996," said Solana, the first NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) chief ever to visit neutral Sweden.
"No decision will be taken this year about enlargement," he added.
Solana, in Sweden for a day before heading to Finland, said several processes were underway consecutively to prepare a new European security model for the post Cold War era.

New democracies from the former Soviet Union bloc are seeking to ensure their position in the new framework either through membership of NATO or NATO's Partnership for Peace (PfP) which boosts multilateral security links.
Solana said talks with Russia over a planned document on future relations, which would include mechanisms for consultations and cooperation, were part of the whole process.
"We see this as a convergence process," Solana said.
"I would like to have these processes converging towards a summit that will take place in about a year. All this I would like to see happen in the middle of 1997."

The plan by NATO to seal a charter with Russia runs parallel with plans for eastward enlargement of the 16 member alliance, due to be settled by 1999, NATO's 50th anniversary. Russia cannot be frozen out of any successful future pan-European security arrangement.

Although Moscow has denounced NATO plans, saying an enlarged NATO could threaten Russia's national security, it does want a deal to guarantee its interests in the post-expansion period - and NATO wants to formalise the relationship.
"There is no relationship between the enlargement and the bilateral relations with Russia," Solana said.
Solana said no firm decisions would be made on enlargement until 1997 - even though widely tipped for early membership are Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovenia.

He refused to be drawn on the possible membership chances of the Baltic states, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which gained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991 and are now in the queue of countries hoping to join NATO.
"A decision on who will join NATO will be taken by the 16 countries who belong to NATO and nobody else," Solana said.
"The decision will be made in the middle of 1997."
NATO has been pushing an extended version of PFP, known as Super PFP or PFP Plus, for countries not admitted to NATO or who do not want to join NATO, maintaining neutrality.

The PFP was set up two years ago, largely to bolster links with emerging democracies eager to shelter under the alliance's security shield and boost non-members' military cooperation and political contact with NATO.
It now has 27 member nations including neutral Sweden, Austria and non-aligned Finland. Another declared neutral country, Switzerland, on Wednesday announced it was joining the PFP.
